rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports from the new astronomy that the sun is stationary at the world's center and other bodies move around it, with successful eclipse predictions, show that traditional astronomical models are not certain.
rows.anchor: الشمس ساكنة لا تتحرك أصلا وأنها مركز العالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variation of night and day may mean their waxing and waning as the sun's relative nearness and distance change over the seasons.
rows.anchor: تفاوتهما بإزدياد كل منهما بإنتقاص الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may instead refer to local differences in day and night lengths and to different places simultaneously having night, day, morning, noon, or afternoon because Earth is spherical.
rows.anchor: كرية الأرض تقتضي أن يكون بعض الأوقات في بعض الأماكن ليلا

rows.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi describes seven layered earths, each beneath a heavenly dome, with Earth spread flat beneath the sky and celestial bodies arranged across the heavens.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى بعد أن خلق الفلك المكوكب في جوف الفلك الأطلس خلق الأرض سبع طبقات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author inclines to a spherical Earth while acknowledging Ibn Arabi's visionary account and disagreement between it and the majority of modern scholars and religious scholars.
rows.anchor: والقلب يميل إلى الكرية والله لا يستحيي من الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No sound Prophetic reports give a fully detailed account of the heavens and Earth, since such detail is not among the Lawgiver's main concerns; what matters is clear.
rows.anchor: لم يجيء في الأحاديث الصحيحة المرفوعة ما يفصل أمر السموات والأرض أتم تفصيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night is explained as a collective singular whose singular is layla, though other lexicographers regard it as a singular with no attested plural; the author rejects the plural-of-plurals analysis.
rows.anchor: والليل واحد بمعنى جمع وواحده ليلة مثل تمرة وتمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The delayed noun of إن is لآيات; its prefixed lām reflects its position after the predicate, and its indefinite form magnifies the signs, with a plural of paucity serving for abundance.
rows.anchor: وهو أسم إن وقد دخله اللام لتأخره

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One interpretation sees the plural of paucity as hinting that visible signs, however numerous, are few beside the hidden signs in the treasuries of knowledge and unseen realms.
rows.anchor: إلا أنها قليلة في جنب ما خفى منها في خزائن العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People of sound intellect are those whose minds are free of the impurities of sense and conjecture; the root لبّ has differing verb forms among Hijazis and Najdis.
rows.anchor: لأصحاب العقول الخالصة عن شوائب الحس والوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited report uses لبّ for the finest camels, illustrating the word's sense of a pure or choice core.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى منع مني بني مدلج لصلتهم الرحم وطعنهم في ألباب الإبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Changes in the heavens and Earth entail origination and dependence on an eternal agent, establishing a maker and then divine oneness; their precise order also establishes perfect knowledge and power.
rows.anchor: لتغيرها المستلزم لحدوثها وإستنادها إلى مؤثر قديم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Theologians use two arguments from these signs for a Creator: change and possibility; most prefer the argument from possibility.
rows.anchor: الأكثرون على ترجيح الثاني والبحث مفصل في موضعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says these three signs represent heavenly, earthly, and composite phenomena; another ties them to change in an entity, its parts, and external configurations, but that latter account relies on philosophers' matter and form and is unsuitable as a basis for Qur'anic explanation.
rows.anchor: وأعترض بأنه مبني على مذهب الحكماء في إثبات الهيولي والصورة والأوضاع الفلكية

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: The author favors the explanation that this passage stresses God's exclusive sovereignty and power, so it selects three major signs; al-Baqara adds signs of mercy because it also stresses God's wide mercy.
rows.anchor: ما قاله شيخ الإسلام في عدم التعرض لماذكر في تلك السورة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that Quraysh asked Jews and Christians about Moses' and Jesus' signs, then asked Muhammad to turn al-Safa into gold; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: عصاه ويده بيضاء للناظرين وأتوا النصارى فقالوا

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha recounts the Prophet praying through the night and weeping in standing, bowing, and prostration; he said he was a grateful servant and warned against reciting these verses without reflection.
rows.anchor: عن عطاء قال قلت لعائشة رضي الله تعالى عنها أخبريني بأعجب ما رأيت

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report from Ali says that when the Prophet rose at night he used a toothstick, looked toward the sky, and recited the verse.
rows.anchor: على ما روى عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه إذا قام من الليل تسوك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says that while staying with his aunt Maymuna, he saw the Prophet wake around midnight, wipe sleep from his face, and recite the final ten verses of Al Imran.
rows.anchor: بت عند خالتي ميمونة فنام رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance is not accepted from people persisting in sins when death arrives and they see the irreversibility of return and the Angel of Death; saying 'I repent now' is not treated as genuine repentance.
rows.anchor: بأن شاهد الأحوال التي لا يمكن معها الرجوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural 'sins' reflects repeated occurrence over an extended time rather than all categories of sin; the previously mentioned evil is one type of sin.
rows.anchor: وجمعت بإعتبار تكرر وقوعها في الزمان المديد لا لأن المراد بها جميع أنواعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse says 'he said' rather than 'he repented' to avoid counting this last-moment utterance as repentance; the conditional clause after حتى marks the limit of the preceding denial.
rows.anchor: لإسقاط ذلك عن درجة الإعتبار والتحاشي عن تسميته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dying state resembles the afterlife, which begins with death: this world is a place of action without requital, while the next is requital without action.
rows.anchor: الدنيا دار عمل ولا جزاء والآخرة دار جزاء ولا عمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second group is also denied acceptance; mentioning them alongside last-moment repenters warns that delayed repentance is nearly worthless, and repeating the negative may suggest its futility is even more emphatic.
rows.anchor: بكون حال المسوفين في عدم إستتباع الجدوى أقوى من حال

rows.speaker: أكثر أهل العلم
rows.claim: Most scholars understand the first group to include sinful believers and disbelievers, and the second group to mean disbelievers only.
rows.anchor: أن المراد ( بالذين يعملون السيئات ) ما يشمل الفسقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations take both groups as disbelievers, both as sinners with 'disbelievers' used for severity, or both as including the two groups with the label based on predominance.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد بالموصولين الكفار خاصة وأن يراد بهما الفسقة وحدهم

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ and Abu al-Aliya report that the preceding repentance verse concerned believers, this verse's first group hypocrites, and its final group polytheists; the author calls this weak because persistent hypocrites cannot repent, while repentant ones are no different from others.
rows.anchor: أن الآية الأولى نزلت في المؤمنين والثانية في المنافقين والثالثة في المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is evidence that repentance at the point of despair is not accepted, but scholars dispute whether such repentance remains valid while hope, regret, and resolve to stop are possible.
rows.anchor: وأستدل بالآية على أن توبة اليائس كإيمانه غير مقبول وفي المسألة خلاف

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some distinguish repentance from faith: repentance renews an existing covenant with God and may be accepted at despair, while faith initiates a new covenant; the Bazzaziyya calls acceptance of repentance, unlike faith, the sound position.
rows.anchor: لأن الرجاء باق ويصح معه الندم والعزم على الترك

rows.speaker: القاضي عبدالصمد الحنفي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi ʿAbd al-Samad al-Hanafi says Sufis hold that faith still benefits at the sight of punishment; Ibn al-ʿArabi likewise validates faith under compulsion, and Ibn ʿUmar hoped well for a polytheist who gurgled Islam.
rows.anchor: أن مذهب الصوفية أن الإيمان أيضا ينتفع به عند معاينة

rows.speaker: أبو ذر
rows.claim: A report from Abu Dharr says God accepts repentance or forgives a servant until the veil falls; the Prophet explains that the veil falls when the soul departs while the person is still an idolater, supporting repentance before that point.
rows.anchor: تخرج النفس وهي مشركة ولا يخفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse appears to support rejection of last-moment repentance; some answer that it denies guaranteed acceptance rather than guaranteeing rejection, leaving the matter under God's will, while 4:48 excludes the persistent disbeliever from forgiveness.
rows.anchor: أن قبول توبة المسوف والمصر غير متحقق ونفي التحقق غير تحقق النفي

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the dying sinner only says 'I repent now' without true repentance; even if قال has another rhetorical purpose, the word 'now' may show that resolve not to return, a condition of valid repentance, is absent.
rows.anchor: لأن فيه رمزا إلى عدم العزم على عدم العود إلى ما كان عليه من الذنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The referent of 'those' in the punishment clause is parsed as the two groups mentioned, and the preparation of painful punishment is rendered with emphasis on its being readied for them.
rows.anchor: أي المذكورون من الفريقين المترامي حالهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A lexical explanation says أعتدنا means أعددنا, with the dāl changed to tāʾ; the adjective painful intensifies the punishment, and the indefinite noun magnifies it.
rows.anchor: أعددنا فأبدلت الدال تاءا عذابا أليما

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites use the verse to argue that believers who die with major sins unrepented must be punished; the response is that preparing Hell does not state that God will certainly admit them, and may mean punishment if He does not pardon them.
rows.anchor: وأستدل المعتزلة بالآية على وجوب العقاب لمن مات من مرتكبي الكبائر

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ says the verse was abrogated by 4:48, which says God forgives what is below associating partners to whom He wills.
rows.anchor: عن الربيع أن الآية منسوخة بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The abrogation claim is rejected because أعتدنا is a report, and reports are not abrogated.
rows.anchor: خبر ولا نسخ في الأخبار

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An alternative reading makes 'those' refer only to those who die as disbelievers, or to both groups understood as hypocrites first and polytheists second.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى الذين يموتون وهم كفار فلا إشكال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After commanding the Prophet to warn the people who may become pious, God forbids doing so in a way that would lead him to expel the poor believers.
rows.anchor: لما أمر النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بانذار المذكورين لعلهم ينتظمون في سلك المتقين نهى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some accounts suggest the warning and no-expulsion verses came down together, while others do not indicate that.
rows.anchor: ويفهم من بعض الروايات أن الآيتين نزلتا معا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports Quraysh leaders seeing Suhayb, Ammar, Bilal, Khabbab, and other poor Muslims with the Prophet and demanding their expulsion, promising they might then follow him; the Quran was revealed concerning this.
rows.anchor: مر الملأ من قريش على

rows.speaker: خباب
rows.claim: Khabbab reports that al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyayna looked down on the poor believers and demanded private access for tribal leaders, promising to meet the Prophet with the poor later; after Gabriel delivered the verse, the Prophet called the believers to him and then stayed with them when rising.
rows.anchor: جاء الأقرع بن حابس التميمي وعيينة بن حصن الفزاري

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima reports that Quraysh nobles asked Abu Talib to have Muhammad expel poor slaves and allies so they would follow him; Umar suggested doing so temporarily, and verses warning and identifying the grateful were revealed, after which Umar apologized.
rows.anchor: مشى عتبة وشيبة أبنا ربيعة وقرظة بن عبد عمرو

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: The report names the poor believers as Bilal, ʿAmmar, Salim, Subayh, Ibn Masʿud, al-Miqdad, Waqid, ʿAmr, and Marthad, with allies and freedmen among them.
rows.anchor: وكانوا بلالا وعمار بن ياسر وسالم مولى

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: The report says the verse 'Thus We have tried some of them by others' addressed Quraysh leaders and their clients; when it came, Umar apologized, and 'When those who believe in Our signs come to you' was revealed.
rows.anchor: وكذلك فتنا بعضهم ببعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ghadah derives from ghudwah with the waw changing to alif; al-ashi derives from ashwa with waw changing to ya and assimilation. The author says al-ashi appears singular like ashiyyah, though some call it a plural.
rows.anchor: وأصل العشي عشوى قلبت الواو ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say al-ashi is a plural of ashiyyah, but the author finds this far-fetched; morning means early morning or the time from dawn prayer until sunrise, and evening means the end of the day.
rows.anchor: هو جمع عشية وفيه بعد ومعنى الأول لغة البكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Morning and evening can denote continual practice, or the acts of supplication, prayer, remembrance, or Qur'an recitation; the temporal terms can stand for what occurs at those times, and prayer can also mean its time or place.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالدعاء حقيقته أو الصلاة أو الذكر أو قراءة القرآن أقوال

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets morning and evening as the dawn and afternoon prayers; the times are named for the prayers, which are singled out for their honor.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد أنهما عبارة عن صلاتي الصبح والعصر

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmir, also in al-Kahf, and several other readers recite الغدوة with a wāw; Abu ʿUbayd calls that reading an error because he treats ghudwah as a proper name that cannot take the article.
rows.anchor: ابن عامر هنا وفي الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Abu Ubayd criticism: ghudwah is also attested as a common noun with the article, as reported from al-Khalil by Sibawayh, al-Mubarrad, and other language authorities; the transmitted reading itself suffices as evidence.
rows.anchor: منكرا مصروفا فتدخلها أل حينئذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not establish that the Prophet actually expelled anyone; reports say he considered assigning separate times to the devoted poor and Quraysh leaders to draw the latter toward faith, without humiliating the believers.
rows.anchor: والذي تحكيه اة ثار أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام هم أن يجعل لاولئك الداعين المتقين وقتا خاصا

rows.speaker: المشهور
rows.claim: The common interpretation takes God's face as His essence, hence the believers seek Him sincerely; the author notes that this interpretation must explain how God can be willed if will attaches only to possible things.
rows.anchor: فقيل وهو المشهور إنه الذات أي مريدين ذاته تعالى

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj interprets God's face as the direction or path He commands them to seek.
rows.anchor: المراد به الجهة والطريق والمعنى مريدين الطريق

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes seeking God's face as a metaphor for love and seeking His approval; the author says this account is questionable.
rows.anchor: إنه كناية عن المحبة وطلب الرضا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The word 'face' may be used for honor or emphasis, as in expressions such as 'the face of an argument'; the believers seek God in this sense.
rows.anchor: هذا وجه الرأي وهذا وجهه الدليل والمعنى يريدونه

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: The plural pronoun in 'their account' refers to the poor believers, as reported from ʿAṭāʾ and most commentators; grammatically, من is an added marker of comprehensiveness, and the clause interrupts the prohibition to support it.
rows.anchor: ضمير الجمع للموصول السابق كما روي عن عطاء وغالب المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers' faith and deeds are not the Prophet's concern to judge; he must apply rulings to outward appearances and leave hidden accounts to God, against the taunts resembling Noah's people's complaint.
rows.anchor: وإنما وظيفتك حسبما هو شأن منصب الرسالة النظر إلى ظواهر الأمور

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets the account as their provision: their poverty would not harm the Prophet, so it cannot justify expelling them.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن زيد أن المعنى ما عليك شيء من حساب رزقهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads the two reciprocal denials as one thought like 'no bearer bears another's burden'; the author objects that this is not a fitting reading of the Qur'anic wording.
rows.anchor: ان الجملتين في معنى جملة واحدة تؤدي مؤدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting 'upon you' in both clauses may honor the Prophet or emphasize that the believers' account is not exclusively his responsibility.
rows.anchor: للتشريف له عليه أشرف الصلاة وأفضل السلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Some commentators, including a report from Ibn Abbas, take the plural pronoun to mean the idolaters: the Prophet is not accountable for them, so concern for their conversion cannot prompt him to expel believers.
rows.anchor: وروي ذلك عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما والمعنى إنك لا تؤاخذ بحسابهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in 'then you would expel them' refers to the believers under either reading; the subjunctive presents expulsion as a consequence ruled out by the preceding denial.
rows.anchor: للمؤمنين على كل حال والفعل منصوب

rows.speaker: الإمام والزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari allow 'then you would be among the wrongdoers' to coordinate with the preceding consequence, since expelling the believers would cause wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: على وجه التسبب لأن الكون ظالما معلول طردهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author answers that injustice through expulsion ceases when expulsion is negated, so the coordinated clauses share the same cause for their subjunctive form.
rows.anchor: فانتفاء الظلم بالطرد يتوقف على ذلك أيضا فيلزم من الانتفاء الانتفاء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An objection says the coordination implies that expulsion would not be wrong if the Prophet were accountable for them; the reply reads the denial as saying that lack of responsibility is why expulsion would wrong them.
rows.anchor: واعترض أيضا بأن العطف مؤذن بأن عدم الظلم لعدم تفويض الحساب اليه

rows.speaker: الدر المصون
rows.claim: A further parsing makes the first result clause answer the prohibition, but the author finds the literal repetition 'do not expel them and then you would expel them' untenable.
rows.anchor: ولا تطردهم فتطردهم وهو كما ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second denial cannot govern the result if that would imply that expulsion is proper whenever the Prophet bears their account; because that meaning is impossible, the first denial governs.
rows.anchor: إذ يلزم المعنى حينئذ أنه لو كان عليهم شيء من حسابه عليه الصلاة والسلام كان طرده إياهم حسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning that he would be among wrongdoers means wronging himself or those believers, or becoming characterized by injustice.
rows.anchor: فالمراد فتكون من الظالمين لأنفسهم أو لأولئك المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The weighing is the weighing of deeds, distinguishing heavy from light and good from bad; the author parses 'the weight' as the subject, with 'on that day' as its predicate and 'true' as its description.
rows.anchor: أي وزن الأعمال والتمييز بين الراجح منها والخفيف والجيد والرديء

rows.speaker: بعض المعربين
rows.claim: Some grammarians instead make 'true' the predicate and 'on that day' the temporal modifier, avoiding a break between adjective and noun; the author notes that this uses a definite verbal noun in an uncommon way.
rows.anchor: أن ( الحق ) خبر و ( يومئذ ) ظرف للوزن

rows.speaker: الأصفهاني
rows.claim: Al-Isfahani proposes that 'true' is an appositive to the implicit pronoun in the adverb, a sound parsing, though the author favors the first for meaning and the flexibility of adverbs.
rows.anchor: أن ( الحق ) بدل من الضمير المستتر في الظرف

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa offers further parses in which either 'true' answers what the weighing is, or 'weight' is itself the predicate of an omitted subject; the author finds these strained.
rows.anchor: أن يكون ( الوزن ) خبر مبتدأ محذوف أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading substitutes القسط, and al-Raghib defines weighing as determining a thing's measure, commonly with a balance or scales.
rows.anchor: والوزن كما قال الراغب معرفة قدر الشيء

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority, according to al-Qadi, hold that records of deeds are weighed on a balance with a tongue and two pans so people witness justice; the records' true nature is known to God.
rows.anchor: والجمهور كما قال القاضي على أن صحائف الأعمال هي التي توزن بميزان له لسان وكفتان

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
rows.claim: A hadith describes a servant with ninety-nine enormous scrolls of sins, then a card bearing the two testimonies; it outweighs the scrolls, and nothing is heavier than God's name. Al-Hakim authenticated the report.
rows.anchor: يصاح برجل من أمتي على رؤوس الخلائق يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: القرطبي عن الحكيم الترمذي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi, citing al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, says the card is not the basic testimony of monotheism, since scales set opposites against one another and one person cannot have both faith and disbelief; rather, the believer's later utterance is a good deed.
rows.anchor: على ما قاله القرطبي نقلا عن الحكيم الترمذي ليست شهادة التوحيد

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Others allow that the card is the testimony of monotheism, perhaps as a person's final words; they deny that the pans must contain opposites, so the impossibility objection does not follow.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون المراد هذ الكلمة إذا كانت آخر كلامه في الدنيا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: Another report from ʿAbd Allah b. ʿAmr depicts Adam watching descendants go to Paradise or Hell and Muhammad interceding for a member of his community with a tiny white card, identified as the sender's prayers upon the Prophet; it tips the scale and saves him.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله أيضا قال إن لادم عليه السلام من الله عز جل موقفا في فسح من العرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the report about the Prophet's intercession with the tiny card is sound, it magnifies his honored standing before God among all generations.
rows.anchor: ولعل فعل مثل هذا إد صح الخبر مبالغة في اظهار كرامة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A hadith says a huge, heavy man will weigh no more than a mosquito's wing before God; the author questions how this view accounts for the other pan and notes that the report is not explicit proof that persons are weighed.
rows.anchor: من حديث أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه إنه ليؤتى العظيم السمين يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One view attributed to Ibn Abbas says deeds that appear as accidents in this world become fitting substances in the next; several authorities regard this as sound doctrine.
rows.anchor: وروي هذا عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما وصححه غير واحد

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi reports that a person's deeds are placed in the scale, then cloud-like knowledge he taught people is placed in the other pan and tips it; Hammad b. Sulayman reports a similar account.
rows.anchor: عن إبراهيم النخعي قال يجاء بعمل الرجل فيوضع بكفة ميزانه يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: مجاهد والأعمش والضحاك
rows.claim: Mujahid, al-Aʿmash, and al-Dahhak, followed by the Muʿtazilites, take weighing as a metaphor for just judgment; some Muʿtazilites allow literal weighing rationally, while others deny it because deeds are nonenduring accidents, weighing has no benefit to an omniscient God, and useless action would be improper.
rows.anchor: الوزن عبارة عن القضاء السوي والحكم العادل

rows.speaker: الآمدي
rows.claim: Al-Amidi objects that justice and fairness cannot be described as heavy or light; a report from Salman explicitly describes a corporeal scale vast enough for the heavens and Earth, which angels ask who could weigh.
rows.anchor: واعترض الآمدي على ذلك بان الميزان موصوف بالثقل والخفة

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that the two pans of the scale are as vast as the heavens and Earth; angels ask who will weigh with it, and God answers that He will weigh whoever He wills.
rows.anchor: خلق الله تعالى كفتي الميزان مثل السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: داود
rows.claim: A tradition says David saw the immense scale and fainted; God told him that if pleased with a servant He could fill a pan with half a date given in charity.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الآثار أن الله تعالى كشف عن بصر داود عليه السلام فرأى من الميزان

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says one should follow the transmitted hadiths about the scale because there is no reason to abandon them for figurative readings.
rows.anchor: فالأولى كما قال الزجاج اتباع ما جاء في الأحاديث

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: In response to the claim that believers already know God's justice and deniers will reject any scale, a scholar says weighing discloses the true realities and qualities of deeds, leaving no doubt that they are the same deeds performed in this world.
rows.anchor: أجيب بأنه ينكشف الحال يومئذ وتظهر جميع الأشياء بحقائقها على ما هي عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural 'balances' may refer to different weighings or weighed items, to an omitted word meaning pans, or to one scale for each deed.
rows.anchor: والموازين إما جمع ميزان وجمعه مع أن المشهور الصحيح أن الميزان مطلقا واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those whose balances are heavy are successful: al-muflihun means those who attain salvation and reward; the plural points to the group, while pronoun and demonstrative forms track grammatical number and distance.
rows.anchor: والجمعية باعتبار معناه كما أن افراد ضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The continuation identifies them as winners of salvation and reward, either with al-muflihun as predicate or as the predicate of a second subject; its definiteness marks the known or prototypical successful people of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: ما يعرفه كل أحد من حقيقة المفلحين وخصائصهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those whose balances are light lose themselves by wasting the innate disposition for Islam that every newborn possesses, or the disposition toward goodness at the root of human nature.
rows.anchor: بتضييع فطرة الاسلام التي ما من مولود إلا يولد عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The causal phrase attaches to 'lost'; the prepositional phrase is advanced for the rhyme, ظلم is construed with ب for its sense of denial, and past plus present verbs indicate continued wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وقدم عليه للفاصلة وعدي الظلم بالباء لتضمنه معنى التكذيب أو الجحود

rows.speaker: بعض
rows.claim: Some say unbelievers too have deeds weighed if those deeds do not depend on Islam; al-Qurtubi calls this correct and says it can lessen their punishment, as with Abu Talib.
rows.anchor: وظاهر النظم الكريم أن الوزن ليس مختصا بالمسلمين بل الكفار أيضا توزن أعمالهم

rows.speaker: الكثير
rows.claim: Many hold weighing is for Muslims only, since unbelievers' works are nullified and cannot lessen their punishment; al-Sakhawi says any mitigation for Abu Talib is a special exception.
rows.anchor: وذهب الكثير إلى أن الوزن مختص بالمسلمين وأما الكفار فتحبط أعمالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage does not address those whose good and bad deeds balance, identified by one opinion as the people of the Heights; some infer such a group does not exist, while a reply places them among those whose deeds are mixed and notes God's asa promises fulfillment.
rows.anchor: وهي على كلا التقديرين ساكتة عن بيان حال من تساوت حسناته وسيئاته

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, with reports from Ibn Abbas and Muqatil, takes each nation's term as an appointed time for its destruction; the statement warns Mecca of punishment at a time known to God.
rows.anchor: أي وقت معين مضروب لاستئصالهم كما قال الحسن وروي ذلك عن ابن عباس ومقاتل

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other interpretations take the term as a set respite before punishment, or as the time of death, construing 'each nation' as each individual of the nation; the author notes the death-time reading needs no omitted wording.
rows.anchor: وفسر بعضهم الأجل هنا بالمدة المعينة التي أمهلوها لنزول العذاب

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: The pronoun 'their' can refer to the nations implied by 'every nation' or to each nation itself; explicit repetition of 'term' emphasizes each community's particular appointed time.
rows.anchor: الضمير كما قال بعض المحققين إما للأمم المدلول عليها بكل أمة

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين
rows.claim: Ibn Sirin recites آجالهم in the plural; Ibn Jinni favors that form, while the singular may denote the class collectively.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن سيرين آجالهم بصيغة الجمع واستظهرها ابن جني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrival of the term means its approach or completion; ساعة is a tiny interval, not the astronomers' fixed hour or the variable hour used by jurists, and the expression means no delay whatsoever, with the form implying incapacity to delay.
rows.anchor: والمراد من مجيء قربه أو تمامه أي إذا حان وقرب أو انقطع وتم

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Hufi and others parse 'nor do they advance' as coordinated with 'nor are they delayed'; an objection says advancing after the term arrives is logically impossible and therefore redundant.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه عطف على ولا يستأخرون كما أعربه الحوفي وغيره

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another parse coordinates the final clause with the conditional premise: each nation has a term, and it cannot advance at any point; al-Salakuti objects that restricting only the no-delay clause to the condition is not readily apparent.
rows.anchor: على الجملة الشرطية لا الجزائية فلا يتقيد بالشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author holds that coordination with the conditional clause is correct: God-determined timing cannot be changed, so the term can neither advance nor be delayed; the pairing also echoes the two kinds of unaccepted late repentance in 4:18.
rows.anchor: والحق العطف على الجملة الشرطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interpretation that they cannot change the appointed time resembles 'no fresh or dry thing except in a record'; scholars also analyze whether a condition preceding the coordinated clause is shared by it.
rows.anchor: ولا رطب ولا يابس إلا في كتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The no-delay clause comes first because the point is that the condemned cannot escape punishment; Yunus reverses the order to explain why destruction is delayed despite their deserving it, following the command to let them enjoy themselves for a while.
rows.anchor: وتقديم بيان انتفاء الاتئخار كما قيل لما أن المقصود بالذات بيان عدم خلاصهم من العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The impure and pure may mean disbelievers and believers, corruption and righteousness, or the money spent by polytheists against the Messenger and money spent by Muslims to support him; the final reading attaches the purpose to making their spending a regret, not to their being gathered.
rows.anchor: أي الكافر من المؤمن أو الفساد من الصلاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, and Yaʿqub read ليميز with doubled yāʾ, a more intensive form than ليميز; an anomalous reading has the criminals told to separate themselves.
rows.anchor: من التمييز وهو أبلغ من الميز لزيادة حروفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root يركمه means to pile together like a piled cloud, sand, or army; if impure means disbelievers, it depicts their crowding, while corruption means sorting each corrupt kind together.
rows.anchor: سحاب مركوم ويوصف به الرمل والجيش أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the impure means hostile spending, God gathers that money to cast its owners into Hell and brand their faces and sides; a broader reading joins evil unbelievers with their evil money to increase their torment and regret.
rows.anchor: وأما المال المنفق في عداوة الرسول صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم وجعله في جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative may point to the impure group or to spenders who remained unbelievers; its distance signals their extreme depravity, and they are complete losers of themselves and their wealth.
rows.anchor: لأنهم خسروا أنفسهم وأموالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'and the three' is coordinated with the mention of the Prophet and shares the verb 'turned'; inserting an implicit 'turned' has been proposed because their repentance differs, but the author finds that unnecessary.
rows.anchor: لتغاير هذه التوبة والتوبة السابقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three were left behind in judgment and their case postponed: no excuse was accepted or rejected until revelation came; the wording may be figurative or imply their case, or it may mean that they themselves stayed behind from the campaign.
rows.anchor: أي خلف أمرهم وأخر عن أمر أبي لبابة وأصحابه حيث لم يقبل منهم معذرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were Kaʿb b. Malik, Hilal b. Umayya, and Murara b. al-Rabiʿ; Muslim and others call Murara al-Amiri, while many hadith scholars correct this to al-Umari.
rows.anchor: وهم كعب بن مالك من بني سلمة وهلال بن أمية من بني واقف ومرارة بن الربيع

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima, Ruzayn b. Hubaysh, and ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd read خلفوا with light lām and explain it as being left behind in Medina or becoming corrupt; ʿAli b. al-Husayn, al-Baqir, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, and al-Sulami read خالفوا, while al-Aʿmash reads المخلفين.
rows.anchor: بفتح الخاء واللام خفيفة أي خلفوا الغازين بالمدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth's constriction marks the end of their delayed case: people shunned them under the Prophet's order, and the image means they could not settle in the world despite its breadth; a cited poetic line evokes the fear of the pursued.
rows.anchor: لأعراض الناس عنهم وعدم مجالستهم ومحادثتهم لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their selves are their hearts; the heart's constriction means grief with no room for joy, and the move from constricted earth to constricted selves heightens the rhetoric.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا ترق من ضيق الأرض عليهم إلى ضيقهم في أنفسهم وهو في غاية البلاغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They knew there was no refuge from God's displeasure except seeking His forgiveness and repenting to Him; ظنوا here means they knew.
rows.anchor: أي عملوا أنلا ملجأ من سخطه إلا إلى استغفاره والتوبة إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's turning to them may mean enabling them to repent, revealing their acceptance in the Qur'an, or repeatedly returning with mercy so they persist in repentance; another view says He accepted their lapse so that they could repent again without despair.
rows.anchor: أي وفقهم للتوبة ليتوبوا أو أنزل قبول توبتهم في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is repeatedly accepting repentance, even if a person returns to sin a hundred times in one day, and mercifully grants blessings despite their deserving punishment.
rows.anchor: لمن تاب ولو عاد في اليوم مائة مرة

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb's account says he missed no campaign except Tabuk, though he had missed Badr without blame because the Prophet had set out for the Quraysh caravan and met the enemy unexpectedly; Kaʿb valued the Aqaba pledge above Badr despite Badr's greater fame.
rows.anchor: سمعت كعب بن مالك يحدث حديثه حين تخلف عن رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم في غزاة تبوك

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb says that before Tabuk he had never been stronger or wealthier and had never owned two mounts for a campaign; the Prophet announced the destination because the journey was long and difficult, the weather hot, and the enemy numerous.
rows.anchor: أنى لم أكن قط أقوى ولا أيسر مني حين تخلفت عنه في تلك الغزاة

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: The Muslim force was so large it had no single register; a would-be deserter thought his absence might remain unknown without revelation, and the expedition began when fruit and shade were appealing.
rows.anchor: كثير لايجمعهم كتاب حافظ يريد الديوان

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb repeatedly went out intending to prepare, returned having done nothing, and delayed until the army departed; although he considered catching up, he never did, and later saw only suspected hypocrites or people excused by God among those left behind.
rows.anchor: فلم يزل ذلك يتمادى بي حتى إنتهوا وتفارط الغزو فهممت أن أرتحل فأدركهم

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: At Tabuk, while seated among his companions, the Prophet asked what had happened to Kaʿb b. Malik.
rows.anchor: ما فعل كعب بن مالك
